newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico business seeks tax reform, better security.
newsitem.headline: Mexico business seeks tax reform, better security.

text.p: Mexican business leaders said on Tuesday they were seeking a wide-ranging tax reform, greater deregulation and better security against crime among top priorities from the government next year.

Hector Larios Santillan, president of the Business Coordinating Council, told reporters he hoped business leaders could agree a big tax reform package by January or February to present to Congress for debate later in the year.
"The government is committed to establishing a tax reform next year to promote jobs and the industrial base," he said.
Changes could include the scrapping of a tax on assets -- already temporarily suspended for small businesses this year and next -- and greater simplification, Larios said.

Among other concerns for Mexican business, public security was a "serious problem" with losses from thefts, assaults and other crimes rising, although recent government initiatives had helped, he added.
1997 was also a crucial political year with major congressional and state elections being held, Larios said.

But, he added, votes held in recent months in Mexico had been held peacefully and with minimal post-electoral rowing between victors and defeated, giving an encouraging sign to businessmen concerned about political risk next year.

Claudio X. Gonzalez, president of the Mexican Businessmen's Council, said the international panorama looked favourable to Mexico next year, with the U.S. -- Mexico's main market -- likely to continue growing and prices for oil -- Mexico's top export -- firm amid rising exports.
Good rain this year also meant Mexico was likely to import less grain in 1997, added Gonzalez, who is also president of Kimberly-Clark Corp's Mexican affiliate.

Referring to the government's 1997 economic programme announced over the weekend after negotiations with business and labour, Larios and Gonzalez said they believed the need for such negotiated programmes was diminishing.
"After 10 years of (economic) pacts, this is the first year when we thought it might not be necessary to conclude a pact," Gonzalez said.
The leaders said the main changes made during this year's negotiations were to persuade the government to reduce the size of the increase it originally proposed in fuel and electricity prices.

Larios said he expected inflation next year to be close to the government's target of 15 percent and forecast that probably 700,000 to 800,000 new jobs would be created in Mexico next year after 600,000 this year.

On exchange rate policy, Gonzalez said Mexico had no choice, but to follow a free floating regime -- although he added that the currency appeared to be stabilising as the realisation spread that "nothing is fundamentally negative" for the currency now.

Larios said businessmen would have liked to have had a higher rise in the minimum salary for next year than the 17 percent agreed, but said companies still struggling with the country's 1995 recession were hard pressed to pay even 17 percent.

"Seventeen percent is a sacrifice for many companies, which are in serious crisis," he said. "...the problem is that generalised rises are unfair because many companies are not in a condition to pay (them)."

Larios estimated that only about five to six percent of the 9.8 million Mexican workers affiliated to the social security plan were on the base minimum salary, but said the minimum wage also served as a benchmark for "professional minimum salaries" covering up to three million workers and contract negotiations covering the remainder.
